management.value: Management/Board: There was a significant and very recent leadership change. Paul Hudson, CEO since 2019, was ousted in Feb 2026 and abruptly replaced after a massive research spending boost failed to deliver rapid results, appointing its first-ever female leader, Belén Garijo. Who is Belén Garijo? Garijo has served as CEO and Chair of the Executive Board of Merck KGaA since 2021. Her appointment marks a return to Sanofi, where she previously spent 15 years — including leading the integration of Genzyme following its acquisition, serving as VP of Pharmaceutical Operations for Europe and Canada, and sitting on Sanofi's Executive Committee. Earlier in her career, she worked in R&D at Abbott Laboratories. Sanofi stated that Garijo's priority will be to "strengthen the productivity, governance, and innovation capacity of R&D." In short, the board is asking her to bring more discipline and rigor to the R&D engine that Hudson built up but struggled to deliver results from. Sanofi shares fell nearly 6% on the announcement of the CEO change, with some analysts pointing to Garijo's relatively low profile.

dossier_sections.text: COMPANY DESCRIPTION: French pure-play biopharma company headquartered in Paris, founded in 1973. Engages in the R&D, manufacturing, and marketing of pharma products, principally in the prescription market. Describes itself as an "R&D driven, AI-powered biopharma company." It applies its deep understanding of the immune system to invent medicines and vaccines across six therapeutic areas: Immunology and Inflammation, Oncology, Rare Diseases, Rare Blood Disorders, and Vaccines. Largest product is Dupixent (dupilumab), a biologic injection developed with Regeneron that treats a range of inflammatory conditions — eczema, asthma, nasal polyps, and more. In 2025, Sanofi Dupixent sales were €15.7 bn in, ~33.6% of total sales of €46.7 bn that year. Sanofi expects Dupixent to reach around €22 bn in annual sales by 2030. Primary patent covering Dupixent’s composition expires around 2031. Sold 50% controlling stake in its consumer Healthcare division (OTC products like cold medicines and vitamins) in Oct 2024 to CD&R providing Sanofi with ~€10 bn in net cash proceeds. Sanofi remains a significant shareholder. 3 biopharma franchises: Specialty Care (high-value drugs like Dupixent, rare disease treatments, oncology, multiple sclerosis) ~45% of rev General Medicines (older established products, including diabetes drugs like Lantus and Toujeo) ~37% of rev Vaccines (through its Sanofi Pasteur subsidiary, the world's largest vaccine producer) ~18% of rev

management.value: Management and capital allocation: The management team is solid, and the company consistently executes near flawlessly. Prior to his appointment in 2018, CEO C.C. Wei was president and co-CEO from 2013, and co-COO for the year prior. From 2009 to 2012, he led business development, and before that he was president of mainstream technology. Before joining TSMC in 1998, he held senior positions at Chartered Semiconductor and ST Microelectronics, and prior to that, he was a member of the technical staff at Texas Instruments in the R&D organization. Wei was awarded the Semiconductor Industry Association’s Robert N. Noyce Award in 2025 (this is the semiconductor industry’s highest honor). Outside of Wei, most other executives have been at TSMC for decades. They have a strong engineering-first culture and proven ability to execute at massive scale. On capital allocation, priorities include reinvesting back into the business, with cap ex dedicated to building out production capacity, and returning excess capital to shareholders with a bias toward dividends. While cap ex spend can fluctuate year to year, it is consistently high on an absolute basis ($41bn in 2025, expected to be $56bn in 2026) and as a percent of total sales (typically in the mid-30s to low-40s range). Cap ex spend topped 50% of total sales just five years ago, in 2021. TSMC has returned more than $117bn USD in dividends to shareholders since 1994, and the current dividend yield is 1.1%. They’ve repurchased $3.2bn in shares over that same time frame. TSMC has historically not been acquisitive.

Basis of competition is leading-edge technology, time to market and reliability, including order accuracy and timeliness. Foundries generally do not compete on price. Massive scale advantages in a highly capital-intensive and extremely technically difficult business coupled with strong customer partnerships make it difficult to compete. TSMC does not design their own chips (compete with customers), which makes them an even more trusted partner. TSMC spent $41bn in cap ex in 2025 and will spend $56bn this year. Their cap ex represents the bulk of industry spend (typically low-40s to mid-60s as a percent of total). Consistent, meaningful investment reinforces their incredibly strong moat.

dossier_sections.heading: Company description
dossier_sections.text: COMPANY DESCRIPTION:In 1987, TSMC pioneered the pure-play foundry business model by focusing solely on manufacturing their customers’ silicon chips. From his time in the industry, founder Morris Chang realized that “fabbing” or manufacturing chips is the pain point in the value chain as it’s expensive and very difficult. By choosing not to design, manufacture or market any semiconductor products under its own name, TSMC never competes directly with customers (in other words, they are chip agnostic). Today, TSMC is the largest semiconductor foundry, manufacturing nearly 13,000 products using hundreds of distinct technologies for hundreds of customers. Annual capacity of the manufacturing facilities managed by TSMC and subsidiaries exceeded 17mn wafers in 2025. Almost all manufacturing is out of Taiwan, but the company does have a presence in the US, China and Japan. They are in process of building out advanced fabs in Arizona. Sales have predominantly been to US customers over the last decade+, at 75% of total sales last year (the US remains dominant in chip design with companies like Apple, Qualcomm, Nvidia, Amazon and Google). Chips manufactured by TSMC cover a wide range of applications in the computer, communications, consumer and industrial segments, and they are used in a variety of end markets including mobile devices (29% of sales), high performance compute, or HPC (58%), automotive (5%), the internet of things, or IoT (5%) and consumer electronics (1%). Apple and Nvidia are their largest customers (17% and 19% of sales, respectively), and top 10 customers represent 78% of total sales. Sales generated from advanced manufacturing processes, defined as 7 nanometer and below, continue to grow as a percent of total business, from 9% of total sales in 2018 (when 7nm was the leading edge) to 75% today.

dossier_sections.text: Why we own TSMC pioneered the pure-play foundry business model by focusing solely on manufacturing their customers’ silicon chips. Today, they are the largest semiconductor foundry, manufacturing nearly 13,000 products using hundreds of distinct technologies for hundreds of customers including Apple, Nvidia, AMD, Qualcomm and AI and cloud players like Google and Amazon. Chips manufactured by TSMC cover a wide range of applications in the computer, communications, consumer and industrial segments, and they are used in a variety of end markets including mobile devices, high performance compute, auto, and consumer electronics. Chips are the building blocks for the digital economy, powering everything from smartphones and computers to datacenters, cars and medical devices, which is a substantial tailwind to the business. Semiconductor industry sales are expected to reach $1.5tn this year and could top $2tn by the end of the decade. With a monopoly on leading edge silicon, derived from their massive scale advantages in a highly capital-intensive and extremely technically difficult business, not to mention their strong customer partnerships, TSMC benefits from the ever-increasing pervasiveness of chips. While the semiconductor industry is inherently cyclical, and Chinese intervention could lead to permanent loss of capital for shareholders, the most advanced modern technology does not exist without TSMC, and it should remain a core position.

dossier_sections.text: Positives - Revenue and net income both set all-time quarterly records, with net income growth (+77.4% YoY) far outpacing revenue growth on operating leverage and a favorable mix shift toward advanced nodes. dossier_sections.heading: Negatives
dossier_sections.text: Negatives - Despite the beat-and-raise, TSM shares fell roughly 4–5% in the days around the release — commentary attributed this to already “priced for perfection” expectations (stock had risen ~50%+ YTD and traded near 20x forward earnings vs. a 5-year average of ~18x) rather than any operational shortfall. 2026 capital expenditure guidance was raised sharply to US$60–64 billion from US$52–56 billion, and TSMC announced a further US$100 billion U.S. investment (total U.S. commitment now ~US$265 billion across up to 10 fabs) — raising investor concern about near-term free-cash-flow compression. Smartphone revenue declined 4% QoQ (22% of total) amid seasonal patterns and pressure on price-sensitive consumer end markets. Inventory days rose by 7 to 87 days, attributed to the 2-nanometer ramp.
